column2: process.env.TZ changing the offset of an ALREADY-STRINGIFIED Date
column5: the TZ wiring is COMPLETE and correct -- __mbunProcNative.setTimeZone (process_base.inc:688) does setenv + WTF::setTimeZoneOverride + DateCache::resetIfNecessarySlow, and node_process_extra.cppm:371 applyTZ calls it from the env Proxy set/delete traps. Measured on the frozen binary with one long-lived Date: the display NAME follows every reassignment (Central European Summer Time -> British Summer Time -> GMT) but the OFFSET and wall clock stay frozen at 'Sat Apr 14 2018 14:34:56 GMT+0200'. Cause is upstream JSC: DateInstance::m_data is a per-object RefPtr<DateInstanceData> and DateInstance::gregorianDateTime() returns the cached local breakdown whenever m_gregorianDateTimeCachedForMS == internalNumber() (DateInstance.h:62-66). DateInstanceData (DateInstanceCache.h:36-52) carries NO timezone epoch, and DateCache::resetIfNecessarySlow only resets the VM-level lookup table, never the RefPtrs already handed out. Needs a JSC patch adding a tz epoch to DateInstanceData -- not reachable from the binding layer

column4: 2 files, but the change is 'make node:fs actually asynchronous'
column5: test-process-getactiverequests.js and -getactiveresources-track-active-requests.js both fire 12 fs.open() calls and then SYNCHRONOUSLY assert the count is 12. That can never hold in mbun because its whole async fs layer is synchronous: bootstrap.cppm:6674 fs.open does `try { const fd = ...__mbunFdNative.open(...); callback(null, fd) } catch (e) { callback(e) }` -- the callback runs before fs.open returns, and every sibling (stat, lstat, readdir, unlink, realpath, rename, copyFile, rm, rmdir, truncate) is written the same way. So there is no in-flight window to report, and _getActiveRequests (node_process_extra.cppm arrayStubs) is a []-stub with nothing to observe. Gaining these 2 files means deferring fs callbacks to a later loop turn, i.e. changing the completion ordering of the entire test-fs-* family plus every bun js/node/fs file -- a lane of its own, with a full-corpus gate. column5: node's contract is that an fs callback runs after BOTH the nextTick queue and the microtask queue of the calling turn. w65/asyncfs fixed the 11 entry points that ran INSIDE the caller's frame, but ~24 siblings (read, write, close, access, realpath, rename, copyFile, rm, rmdir, truncate, ftruncate, utimes, symlink, link, mkdtemp, exists, opendir, statfs, fsync, readv, writev, glob, chown, fchown, lchown, lutimes, futimes, fdatasync, cp) still defer with G.queueMicrotask, and process.nextTick has STRICT PRIORITY over promise microtasks in this runtime -- so their completion still beats a nextTick queued before it, which is backwards from node. Probe: tools scratch p1.js shows 'micro cb tick'. Moving them onto the same batched drain is mechanical (they are one-line queueMicrotask sites), but it re-orders ~24 APIs at once on a surface the whole corpus uses, and no file is known to be gated on it -- so it needs its own before/after round, not a drive-by

column2: fs.promises resolving in the caller's microtask turn
column5: Every fsPromises method is `Promise.resolve().then(() => <sync impl>)`, so the await continuation is a microtask of the CALLING turn: measured, `await fs.promises.stat()` lands before a process.nextTick queued at call time, and before a setTimeout(0) that node's timers phase would have run first. Node resolves from the poll phase. The idiom is textually repeated across ~40 methods rather than funnelled through one helper, so fixing it means either introducing that helper (touching every method) or resolving each from the callback layer's batched drain. The callback layer was fixed first because it is the one with the hard 'never inside the caller's frame' guarantee; promises only get the phase wrong, never the frame
